newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Gulf War compensation held up by oil deal delay - UN.
newsitem.headline: Gulf War compensation held up by oil deal delay - UN.

text.p: A U.N. body in charge of compensation for Gulf War victims called on Tuesday for the implementation of a stalled deal to allow Iraq to sell its oil, saying the delay was holding up its payouts.

The United Nations Compensation Commission announced it had completed assessing claims for damages filed against Baghdad by one million people forced to leave Kuwait or Iraq due to Iraq's occupation of the oil-rich emirate in 1991-92.

A final group of claims in this "forced departure" category, worth $320 million and submitted by 80,450 workers, was approved by the Governing Council of the U.N. reparations fund for Gulf War victims, which ended a two-day meeting on Tuesday.
The Governing Council is composed of the 15 members of the U.N. Security Council.
This last batch of claims brought the total amount awarded for this category of individuals to $3.2 billion for 920,200 people, the Commission said.
But the Geneva-based Commission addded it faced a dramatic funding shortage and was unable to pay out awards this year, mainly due to a delay in implementing the elusive oil scheme.
"The (Governing) Council expressed the view that all parties involved should act in an effective manner towards the expeditious implementation of resolution 986," it said.
"It represents an indispensable step in favour of the compensation of hundreds of thousands of victims of a conflict that occurred more than five years ago," it added.
Under a deal signed last May, delayed since fighting in northern Iraq which triggered U.S. military raids, the cash-strapped Commission would get 30 per cent of Iraqi oil revenues.
Iraq would be allowed to sell $2 billion worth of oil over six months to buy food and medicine.
Carlos Alzamora, executive secretary of the Commission, told reporters earlier he expected the deal to go ahead in December.
"I presume maybe sometime in December. That has been the forecast," he said, making clear he meant a U.N. timetable.

The Commission, set up by the Security Council to compensate direct losses caused by Iraq's invasion and occupation, is processing private, corporate and government claims against Baghdad with an asserted value of more than $200 billion.
The fund was to get $100 million a month from the oil deal.

"We are waiting for implementation of 986 but we are also coordinating efforts among the members of the Governing Council to provide bridging funds in order to allow the Commission to continue in full with its work programme for the next year," Alzamora told a final news conference.
He said the fund would have approved roughly $7 billion in awards to claimants by the end of 1996, but lacked funds to make payments to victims before then.
Regarding "forced departure" claims, he said the Commission had completed processing all 920,000 claims in that category.

"This corresponds to 95 or 96 per cent of the one million people and their families leaving Kuwait or Iraq practically overnight, and therefore losing all their possessions when the hostilities started," he said.
"Some $3.2 billion in awards have been issued to them."
But Alzamora said none of these forced departure awards had been paid out by the Commission due to a lack of funds.

To date, the Commission has only been able to pay out $13.4 million in awards to 4,000 priority claimants seeking compensation for death of a close relative or serious injury. Funds came from government donations and seized Iraqi assets.
